utterances.text: And I think SDA officials were -- became head of the tax department and also the property board of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was any attempt made by the new administration to change officials in general?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There were obviously other job in the municipal administration, particularly non-political jobs. Did the people who had -- was there any attempt made to change the holders of those particular jobs to suit one or other ethnic group, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I take it that your question is about after the elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course that's not clear in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether any such effort to change those positions were made after the elections and after the appointment of the new political officers, or at least Municipal Assembly president, vice-president, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the period after the party elections, when it came to the representatives of the SDA party, there were no changes, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about so far as the commander of the public security station? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, the Municipal Assembly didn't have that function to elect or re-elect, because the chiefs of the police stations were there by virtue of office and chief of the police stations generally. The competence and authority of that was held, invested in the person of the minister of the interior, and at that time the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a man called Alija Delimustafic, and he effected changes but only for the commander of that police. Although previously the commander's name was Savic, I think. I don't know the first name, but he was a Bosniak, a Muslim, and he appointed somebody by the name of Azemir Ceric, who was a representative of the SDA party. Now, the minister did not change the chief. The man who was there before stayed on. His name was Micevic. Or, rather, his surname was Micevic. I forget his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Djuro Micevic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Djuro. Correct, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The power-sharing agreement that you had all entered into, did that work at first properly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you give any illustrations of it working or not working in the first part of 1991, for example?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was appointed president of the Municipal Assembly for Novi Grad, I was elected by the deputies of the Municipal Assembly and there were representatives of the SDA party there too. So that means that in addition to the deputies in the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party you had deputies from the SDA party voting as well. Now, the power -- the power and authority functioned normally. There were decisions that were taken which came under the competence of the municipality itself, or the Municipal Assembly, so there were no special problems in that respect, if that's what you meant. If you meant the SDA deputies or the SDS deputies. If I've understood your question correctly again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, then, if we may. What about the Croatian war? Your municipality, right on the border with Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what effect, if any, did the war in Croatia in 1991 have on Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, it did have an effect. It would be a very good thing if we could take a look at the map now to see where Bosanski Novi is located - Novi Grad as it is called now - that it is at the very border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, and that's a natural border, with the River Una running along it, and that in the country that all of us lived in together formerly there were no borders between the republics except administrative ones. There were no border crossings or anything of that kind at that time. The war that happened happened first of all in Slovenia, and then it spilt over into Croatia, and unfortunately, it had its effect and was reflected on Novi Grad itself with respect to the war going on in the Republic of Croatia, because as I say, we were only divided by the River Una, and across the river is where that unfortunate war was taking place and the horrific things taking place as do in every war. And you could feel that in Bosanski Novi, Novi Grad itself. You could feel the tension. You could feel the fear and anxiety and the general mood of war, and we could feel it coming closer to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put this map on the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do that. It's not a map which is in evidence from what I could see in the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it if it's just for our orientation, although of course the Chamber has still it clearly in its mind. But we could put it on the ELMO so that we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. This map has been marked to a limited extent, in fact, by the witness, but I don't think that's going to affect things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I then suggest is that we take the map of -- which is in evidence of Bosanski Novi and to put that on the ELMO then. But I've forgotten which one -- it's the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a map 527, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 527, you say. I didn't have that in my mind, but could that be put on the ELMO and then the municipality of -- I see already two copies now handled. The one who is first. You're first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Use this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's directly the municipality which can be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the usher would turn to page 2 of exhibit, there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we get the other view, but I -- no. The location of Bosanski Novi in Bosnia is well known to the Chamber by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was a particular incident of concern in your municipality in 1991; is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did that happen? Could you name the place, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, that happened precisely in 1991. I can't recall the exact day, but it was in August or September of 1991, and the place was Kostajnica. It's now a separate municipality, but at the time it was part of the Novi Grad municipality, and what happened was unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we get there, I think we see it at the top of the map, at the very north. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pasic, what happened, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, as you can see on the map, on my left-hand side, if I am looking at this correctly, you have the Republic of Croatia. So in the northern part of the Novi Grad municipality there's a place called Kostajnica. And let me repeat this: Sometime in August or September, I can't remember the exact time, there was bombing or, rather, from some light weaponry from Croatian Kostajnica. There was shooting coming into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the army and the police of the Republic of Croatia, and the Croatian National Guards Corps, as they were called, the ZNG, were active there. They were throwing bombs at Kostajnica, and on that occasion five civilians were killed. Let me repeat: That was sometime in August or September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did the municipality do about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, our authority was very narrow and we were not able to act in those terms. It was not in the competence of the municipality. It could not act in that military aspect. And as president of the Municipal Assembly, I asked that we attempt to preserve the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina because this was an attack on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was still asking the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina to do something to try to prevent these unfortunate events so that innocents would not lose their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as a direct result of this incident you received a personal telephone call from Mr. Izetbegovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Then president of what was then called the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was headed by its president Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, he called me and asked me -- it was an afternoon conversation at my home number -- he asked me what happened, and I explained to him that unrest had broken out in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and that because of that the border was violated of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina because their official police forces and the ZNG fired at the territory of Kostajnica, the municipality of Novi Grad, and the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina from their territory, the territory of the Republic of Croatia. I repeat that on the occasion five civilians were killed. Mr. Izetbegovic heard me out. It was my impression, my subjective impression that he accepted that coldly. I requested that something really be done and that an attempt be made to protect the border. I think that the outcome of that conversation - that conversation because there were other conversations, other contacts - but I think that the outcome of that conversation was that a Special Police Unit was sent to the Novi Grad municipality and for a while they were in that territory, that area I'm talking about. I note that the composition of that force was ethnically mixed. There were Croat, Serb, and Bosniak members of that force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You say there were other conversations. Is this other conversations with Mr. Izetbegovic that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I think that there was perhaps another conversation. I'm not quite sure. A lot of time has passed since then, but I think that there was another conversation. I couldn't be certain about it, but I think that it also referred to this matter that I just briefly tried to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, as this situation with the Croatian war developed, what impact, if any, did it have on Serb-Muslim relationships within your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Novi Grad municipality could not be kept isolated from all of those horrors. As I said, all of the events in the area and in Croatia were reflected in our municipality. I think that we were the first municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina - and I repeat this was in 1991 - who felt all of this. I think that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina actually broke out in April or March 1991. So that the Novi Grad municipality sensed all of these horrors much, much earlier than the other municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, the horrors of war could be felt by the ordinary people. They sensed fear and tension. In a way, people withdrew. There was distrust between the ethnic groups. There was suspicions, fears, and all of this affected also what was going on in the Republic of Croatia earlier, and I think that is well known what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any difficulties with JNA and TO call-ups?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia still existed then, and the Yugoslav People's Army officially was still in existence. They had their Secretariats for National Defence in the municipalities. They operated independently from the Assembly organs in municipalities, but I know that they did conduct mobilisations in 1991, during the war in Croatia. It's no secret that mostly Serbs responded to that particular call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were there any paramilitary difficulties caused by the Croatian war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about those, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: With the events in Croatia, as I have already said, there were no official borders. There was no official division between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. As the war was going on on the other side of the Una River in Croatia, it could happen that someone crossed the republican border crossing to cross over where there were no roads. Perhaps they could happen to cross over with a rifle and cause an incident, regardless of whether the organs of authority knew about that or not. There were certain attempts at criminal offences. This did happen. As you can see on the map, this is a very long area that the municipality occupies, and you can see the map, it's still in front you. On the left side, this long line is actually the border with the Republic of Croatia, so this entire area needed to be physically secured in order to prevent these possible uncontrolled events, but it was difficult to physically secure this. The civilian police at the time simply did not have the means, didn't have the personnel to prevent something like that from happening. Of course, they did make an attempt to do that, and they were deployed at checkpoints on these roads, but things were going on outside of those checkpoints, outside of the roads. Certain small groups or individuals were creating problems to the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were the paramilitary groups picking on any particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Which period are you thinking of? National -- I mean ethnic groups. I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1991, as a result of the Croatian war.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that there is a no colour, race, or ethnic group as far as crime is concerned, and this was happening in the municipality of Bosanski Novi, Novi Grad. If we're thinking of these small groups, paramilitary formations, if I can call them like that, people who are able to carry a soldier's rifle and carry out a certain criminal act or an offence, they were not interested in colour, ethnic groups or political affiliations. There were problems like that, and if -- if that means anything to you, there was an incident that happened, and it unfortunately ended with a murder at the border crossing between Novi Grad municipality and Dvor na Uni. Arriving from the Dvor na Uni municipality, one of those small groups, or a person from such a small group, he had a nickname. His name was Titin, his last name was Betic, he was an ethnic Serb, and when the police responded - and the police was still of mixed composition with the police officers being both of Serb, Croat, and Bosniak ethnicity - this person did not stop. He even tried at the checkpoint, according to the stories and the report of the police station, I wasn't an eyewitness I'm just saying what I heard, he wanted to react by using his rifle and they killed a man in self-defence. I'm just giving this as an unfortunate incident which had such an ending. And these police members from the mixed police forces had to react because their lives were in danger. This was sometime in 1991, sometime in the summer, I cannot really tell you exactly when. Perhaps this was even recorded in some public security station. This case was probably recorded. It is a drastic example that I recall. Unfortunately, there are more such examples where the public security station of Novi Grad had problems with these small groups or individuals who, unfortunately, would come, for the most part, from the direction of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the tape will not allow us to continue until 7.00, so therefore I would like to have a break, but in view of the breaks we had already, the shortest break possible. We will resume at 20 minutes past six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to continue with exactly what I was asking you before the break. Where were these paramilitary formations coming from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: For the most part they came, as I said, from the Republic of Croatia because of the operations which were already under way in the Republic of Croatia, combat operations that were going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What effect, if any, did the formation of the Serb Krajina Republic have on the situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really give a political assessment in view of my function as the president of the Municipal Assembly of the municipality of Novi Grad. I really am not competent to give an assessment on any major political question, but I can note that in that area of Croatia there was a Serb majority population. I'm talking about the municipalities of Dvor, Kostajnica, and some other municipalities which were part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time. I repeat, there were no firm boundaries or borders such as those between sovereign states that are known in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've talked about lawlessness setting in as a result. You've also talked about the inability of the municipal authorities to deal with this lawlessness. Did you receive any insults at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: That is, unfortunately, true if you're thinking about the lawlessness by certain individuals and small groups which committed offences. Some unpleasant things happened to me as well, regardless of the fact that I am an ethnic Serb. Those individuals subjected me to some unpleasant things as president of the municipality of Novi Grad. I had an uncomfortable situation once even when a group, not a formation but a group of people who were mobilised in the Republic of Croatia were unhappy with their status and they expressed their dissatisfaction, thinking that I could help them in some kind of financial aspect. Those people were not educated but they also didn't know that it was not in my competence to help in any way those who were at the time mobilised in the JNA. This was something uncomfortable for me. I wasn't physically mistreated, but it was more on a psychological basis that this abuse manifested itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of violence in May of 1992 in Bosanski Novi, how had the situation deteriorated in the beginning of 1992? So prior to the start of the war, in effect, is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: There were a certain degree of tension both on the Serb and the Muslim side. I'm thinking of ordinary people. There was a distrust. There was a kind of state created where people really couldn't trust each other. They felt insecure. The war was going on in Croatia, and in a way volunteers on the Muslim side would join the Croatian army. On the other hand, we had mobilised Serbs in the then Yugoslav People's Army, and the arrival of both of these people, volunteers from the Muslim Bosniak side and those Serbs who were mobilised in the JNA, when they came on leave, there was tension between those people and tensions were created, and this could be sensed before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If I may add something else: Serb and Muslim villagers lived in a kind of psychosis, in fear. There were night guard services organised both in Serb and in Muslim villages. And I'm saying this because both Serbs and Muslims lived in the territory of the municipality of Novi Grad while there was a very small percentage of Croats living in the municipality; under 1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the referendum in regard to independence? Did that have any adverse effect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I think that when the war started in Croatia -- or actually in Slovenia, then in Croatia, the majority, and I'm thinking of the Serbs, in the territory of Yugoslavia wanted to remain in some kind of common state in which Muslims, Croats, and Serbs would live together. And this, according to what was published in the media, the position of most people, and I'm thinking of ordinary people and in ordinary conversations, it was the desire of Serbs to remain in a common land where both Serbs, Muslims, and Croats would live. Then there was a referendum which was prompted by the SDA party, the Bosniak party. A referendum was held on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, this was a unilateral decision by the SDA, and in a way it created a certain unease amongst the Serbs in view of the fact that the Serbs are a constitutive people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, just as Muslim, Bosniaks, and Croats are. As far as I know, I know that certain political authorities, or certain people involved in politics on behalf of the Serbian people, were opposed to this, and they were not in favour of such a secession and the splitting of Bosnia-Herzegovina without the agreement of the Serbian people. This referendum had a negative effect, and it made the situation worse, a situation that was already quite heated, and this was like pouring more oil onto the flame, and this seemed to fan the flames of war which was already spreading to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was a Crisis Staff formed in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff in the municipality of Novi Grad was formed, but it didn't have a major role of the kind that I learned about later that Crisis Staffs had in other municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you meant the Crisis Staff in the Municipal Assembly, if I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. And following on from that, when was it formed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say what day it was exactly. I think it was in mid-April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did it do anything prior to the outbreak of the war in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: It was formed in mid-April, as I said, and it -- well, there was no need for it to be formed earlier, because there were official institutions still. People worked in the Municipal Assembly, in the Assembly -- and also in the Executive Board, and they both functioned. So there was no need for a Crisis Staff to be formed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Up to what time did all parties continue to attend the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: All the parties throughout that period, the period since the multi-party elections and once they formed the authorities together after the Serb party received 60 per cent and the SDA received about 30 per cent of the vote and the other parties shared the rest amongst them, the SDP and the Reformist Party of Ante Markovic, so all of these parties participated in all the Municipal Assembly sessions in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me ask the same question a slightly different way. When did the SDA representatives cease participating in the Municipal Assembly, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Once certain incidents occurred and once armed conflicts also erupted in the municipality, it was no longer possible to schedule Municipal Assembly sessions, and that is when the Crisis Staff began to function, which actually in that period substituted for the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first clash in the municipality occurred on the 10th/11th of May of 1992. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was an incident in the Blagaj village; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: That night, on the night between the 10th and 11th of May, 1992, the military police of the TO staff, while they were touring the area, were going from Novi Grad in the direction of Prijedor. At some seven or eight kilometres from Novi Grad there is the village of Blagaj, which is almost 100 per cent inhabited by Muslim Bosniaks, and an incident occurred. As the military police patrol was passing by, unidentified persons fired at their vehicle and lightly wounded two police officers. From that point on, the tension which had still not resulted in anything happening actually then erupted, and the military or the armed conflict actually escalated from that point on in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you get to hear of the incident that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, that night I slept in my own home, which is, as you go towards Kostajnica, on the opposite direction -- in the opposite direction geographically, and the Territorial Defence phoned me up and told me that the incident had taken place in the village of Blagaj, and that on that occasion two military policemen were involved and that it was night-time. It was 11.00 or 12.00 at night, late at night. And of course I got up and went to the staff headquarters, the Territorial Defence Staff headquarters, which is about ten kilometres away from my own home, in the town itself. When I arrived, I called the president of the SDA party, Izet Muhamedagic, to come so we could see what we could do together to deal with the situation that had arisen and to try and calm tensions and to try and stop the shooting and to prevent it from escalating and spreading. And Mr. Muhamedagic, the president of the SDA, did arrive when I called him, and we decided at the headquarters there of the Territorial Defence to try and draft a joint text. I and Mr. Muhamedagic read it out at the opening of the Novi -- local radio, and we tried to lessen the tensions, to calm the mood down, to prevail upon both sides, and to try and settle the situation peacefully. And I have to say that Mr. Muhamedagic, his conduct was very proper, and he did appeal to the members of the SDA party and to everybody else, all the other Bosniaks in Novi Grad, to refrain from any excessive behaviour, any shooting or anything else which could make the situation in the municipality worse. I delivered a similar speech. As president of the Municipal Assembly, I prevailed upon the public too. I asked the Serb population not to react to provocations of this kind and that it would be the regular law enforcement organs, the public security station and the Territorial Defence Staff would deal with the situation and try and find a solution to it peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the violence escalate?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, that night the situation did actually calm down, and we felt that we would be successful in prevailing upon the population over the radio, our appeals over the radio, my own and Mr. Muhamed Agic's, to keep calm. But on the second day, and I think that would be the 11th of May, sometime in the afternoon there was shooting again. I can't say now what direction the shooting came from and who fired first, who started the shooting first. That would be unrealistic of me now. But anyway, the shooting did start up again in the afternoon of the 11th of May, and it went on into that second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when, if at all, was the situation brought under control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Josse. I want to stay within the time line of these events. Regarding the Crisis Staff, who took the initiative, and for what reason exactly, to set up the Crisis Staff? Were instructions received from the outside? How did it happen exactly? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the function, as I understood it, of the Crisis Staff was to endeavour to place under control or to be a link between the Territorial Defence Staff and the public security station and the other municipal organs who were independent to a certain extent or autonomous. So the function of the Crisis Staff was to attempt -- and in fact, the people in the Crisis Staff, by virtue of their position - such as the chief of the public security station, the commander of the TO, the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, members of the Executive Board, the president of the Municipal Assembly - all these people, by virtue of their post and function, were members of the Crisis Staff as well. So that when the situation was heated, when tensions were high, as I've already said I'm not quite sure of the date but I think it was in mid-April, that the Crisis Staff held, well, let's say its first meeting which was of an informative nature, to inform the people of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was who took the initiative of creating, of establishing the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand your question. How do you mean "initiative"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who decided that the Crisis Staff was to be established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the decision -- it was like this: The Crisis Staff, I think we received some instructions and guidelines. I can't remember when, at what time in particular, but there were certain instructions that came from, I think, the party. I think that's it. The Serbian Democratic Party. And let me repeat: The situation was highly tense, and the unrest had already started. Not only in Novi Grad but on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. The war had already started in Sarajevo in that month of April. And in Bosanski Brod, for example, there was war going on. There was shooting. There were casualties. They were killed. So we tried to prevent all this, to stop it from happening in our part. So that's when the Crisis Staff started working and performing the function that it in fact did perform. I don't know if I've explained the situation, but that's how I understood your question and the initiative that you asked about. I think it came from the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can help, Your Honour, this way: Could the exhibits bundle be handed out, please. Your Honours, 1 in that bundle is a report on the work of the Bosanski Novi Municipal Crisis Staff. It's undated. It's signed by this witness. Could I mention in passing, the Court should now have, separately, a translation which is described as unrevised. I am grateful to my learned friend Mr. Harmon. The position is this: That we did submit this document just over a week ago to the CLSS. No translation had been forthcoming. I served the document on him later, I'm bound to say, a few days ago, and just prior to Mr. Pasic commencing his evidence, Mr. Harmon informed me that he had obtained, through his translators, this unrevised translation, and that's clearly going to make our life very much easier. So could I say I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, Mr. Josse, I take it that where the translation says it's Mr. Panic it's due to the bad quality of page 7 that it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I hadn't spotted that, Your Honour, but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you asked whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We should check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if everything would be perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have got tab 1 there, Mr. Pasic. It's a report on the work of the Municipal -- Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Bosanski Novi. Could you turn to the last page, please. In block capitals at the very bottom of page 7, we see three words. What do those three words say?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: It says, "President of the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what do the two words at the very bottom of the page say?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: It says "Radomir Pasic" underneath that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in fact I hadn't asked you this question previously, and I should have done: It's right that you became the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I was going to deal with this document at a later stage, but it's convenient to begin to deal with it now. It doesn't appear to be dated. Are you able to help us as to when you compiled this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I would really have to read through this document in order to be able to see whether it is what it says it is, and at the end here -- well, unfortunately, there's no signature of mine. It says president of the Crisis Staff, Radomir Pasic. I don't know, perhaps it's just my copy. There are a lot of pages and I wouldn't like to hazard an answer, just looking at it at first glance like that, to say what it is. Quite possibly it's all correct, but until I read through it, I wouldn't be able to give you a valid answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two things on that. First of all, this may be my fault, but I thought you had had an opportunity to read it before you commenced your evidence. If the answer to that is -- I'm asking that as a matter of information. I don't think anyone is going to hold it against you one away or another. Had you had an opportunity to read it in the last two days since you've arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: The report on the work of the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Bosanski Novi, as it says here, really did exist. The report was tabled to the Municipal Assembly, but really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, a quite simple question is put to you, whether you had an opportunity to read it prior to coming to this court when you arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document, the report on the work of the Crisis Staff, I have read, yes, but I don't know whether that's this, whether it's this here. If that is indeed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who gave it to you to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report on the work of the Crisis Staff? Well, it still exists. It exists now in the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the questions. You said you did read the document. Who gave that document to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's this document, you put some doubt on that. You said that you have read a document. Same title, the document you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just want to say or, rather, I'm only saying is this the same document that I received from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, from whom did you receive the document that you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Defence. From the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I take it that you do not present any other documents to the Court at this moment and to the witness that -- and so please proceed. Mr. Josse says that the document that was given to the Defence is the same document as the Court and you have in front of you at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The second point I was going to make is perhaps -- I'm going to ask a few questions about it now, but perhaps the witness can take it away with him, because I think he may have another copy, and read it overnight at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that we could produce a copy, although you're the one who --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter is then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- we can provide the copy if we're allowed to have contact via the Victim and Witness service to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, Mr. Harmon, there are no objections to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, doing the best that you can, do you recall when this report was prepared? If you don't remember, say so. I ask that because it's undated.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's no date here. I assume that it was at the first session of the Municipal Assembly that was held after these events, and I think that was sometime in mid-June, although I can't be quite sure about that. I can't remember the day, but I think it was in June. In fact, you can see on the basis of what it says here, the chronological order of events, what was recorded, the events recorded, and I think that that would be the right date when this report on the work of the Crisis Staff was written. There was a bit of a misunderstanding. I didn't mean to create one, but all I wanted to do was confirm or, rather, to explain to you that that was precisely the report that I had before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you personally write this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Not I personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, explain to us the process of its production, bearing in mind it purports to bear your name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: How this report came into being, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. The mechanics of it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, I assume it was sometime in mid-June 1992 when this report was written, so that's a period of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there. Could you please look at the last page, page 7. Approximately in the middle of the page. Reference is made to a date in July, or doesn't it make reference to a time at 1800 hours at the 2nd of July, or is that a mistake in the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're looking at the same thing, it says here 1/2. I think it says June, the sixth month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would look at the last portion of the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take a moment to read through it, just a brief moment, just that particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately the middle of the page. Before we have a blank line, two lines above that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It says here, "At the latest by 0800 hours on the 2nd of June to establish control in the town," in the sense of public law and order and security in the town. And that referred to -- let me just read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say this was June. It's not a very good copy, but I think it's June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sixth month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a translation problem. You noticed that. The translation says July and -- DEFENCE COUNSEL: I'm grateful to Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could -- because if I compare the reference to June in this same typewriting machine -- let me not speculate on that, but it seems that the Cyrillic N and the Cyrillic L are quite different, but let's not speculate on that. You're invited to further explore that matter. I hope it's not a courtesy by Mr. Harmon that created the problem, the translation being unrevised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would ill behoove me to even suggest any form of criticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it is 7.00 already. Perhaps we continue with the document tomorrow. Then the witness will have had an opportunity to read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm anxious -- I'll do it in the morning to continue with Judge Hanoteau's questions and deal with the first paragraph of that document, but I'm happy to do that at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then perhaps the witness has a copy of the document. That's the whole of the bundle at this moment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're having one made at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's being made at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see even it's brought in, although -- Mr. Pasic, we'll finish for today. You'll be provided now with a copy of the B/C/S version. Could you please return the bundle of documents to Madam Usher so that it will be given to you, if need be, tomorrow again. Madam Usher. And you're invited to read over the copy of the documents. Mr. Pasic, I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give during the days to come. I would like to see you back in this same courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of December, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
